_link.title: I can determine the direction of the force on a moving charged particle using the right-hand slap rule, accounting for the sign of the charge

toLevel2.stem: When using the right-hand slap rule for a moving charge, the thumb points in the direction of:
distractors: The magnetic field lines in the region
The force on the charged particle itself
Electron flow through the magnetic field

toLevel2.stem: An electron moves to the right through a field directed into the page. The right-hand slap rule gives an upward force for a positive charge. What is the force on the electron?
distractors: Upward
To the left
Into the page

toLevel2.stem: Why must the force direction be reversed when applying the right-hand slap rule to an electron?
toLevel2.answer: Because the electron has a negative charge
distractors: Because electrons are lighter than protons
Because electrons move faster than protons
Because electrons create stronger fields

toLevel2.stem: When applying the right-hand slap rule, the fingers point in the direction of the:
distractors: Electric current
Force on particle
Velocity of charge

toLevel2.stem: A proton moves upward through a magnetic field directed to the right. Using the right-hand slap rule, the force on the proton is directed:
distractors: Into the page
To the left
Downward

toLevel2.stem: For a negative charge, the force direction is {{blank:1}} to the direction given by the right-hand slap rule for a {{blank:2}} charge.
In the right-hand slap rule, the thumb represents {{blank:1}} current and the palm push represents the {{blank:2}}.
The right-hand slap rule directly gives the correct force direction for a {{blank:1}} charge, but must be {{blank:2}} for an electron.
The right-hand slap rule gives the force direction directly for a positive charge without any reversal needed.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A proton and an electron moving in the same direction through the same field experience forces in the same direction.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why does a proton deflect in the opposite direction to an electron when both move through the same magnetic field in the same direction?
toLevel3.answer: They have opposite charges, so the force on each is in the opposite direction
distractors: The proton is heavier so gravity pulls it in a different direction from the electron
The electron creates a stronger magnetic field that opposes the external field lines
The proton moves slower than the electron so the force acts for a longer time period

toLevel3.stem: A student applies the right-hand slap rule to an electron moving left through a field directed upward and gets a force out of the page. What is the actual force on the electron?
toLevel3.answer: Into the page, because the electron's negative charge reverses the direction
distractors: Out of the page, because the right-hand rule gives the correct answer directly
Upward, because the force must be parallel to the magnetic field for electrons
To the right, because the force opposes the electron's direction of travel here

toLevel3.stem: Conventional current flows in the opposite direction to electron flow. How does this affect the use of the right-hand slap rule for electrons?
toLevel3.answer: The thumb must point opposite to the electron's velocity, and the resulting force direction is correct without further reversal
distractors: The thumb points in the same direction as the electron's velocity and the result is correct
The rule cannot be used for electrons at all because they flow opposite to convention
The thumb points in the electron's direction and then the result must be reversed twice

toLevel3.stem: A positive ion moves downward through a field directed out of the page. Using the right-hand slap rule, the force on the ion is directed:
distractors: To the right
Upward
Into the page

toLevel3.stem: An electron moves into the page through a field directed upward. What is the direction of the force on the electron?
distractors: To the left
Downward
Out of the page

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important to account for the sign of the charge when determining the force direction on a moving particle?
toLevel3.answer: The force direction reverses for negative charges, which changes the path the particle takes
distractors: The magnitude of the force depends on whether the charge is positive or negative overall
Negative charges do not experience any magnetic force so the rule does not apply to them
Positive and negative charges always move in the same direction regardless of their sign

toLevel3.stem: To use the right-hand slap rule for an electron, point the thumb {{blank:1}} to the electron's velocity, representing the direction of {{blank:2}} current.
A proton and an electron enter the same field in the same direction. The proton is deflected {{blank:1}} while the electron is deflected in the {{blank:2}} direction.
The sign of the charge determines the {{blank:1}} of the magnetic force, but does not affect its {{blank:2}}.
When using the right-hand slap rule for an electron, you can point the thumb opposite to the electron's velocity and the palm push gives the correct force directly.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: An electron moves to the right at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s through a 0.30 T field directed out of the page. Determine the direction and magnitude of the force.
distractors: Upward, 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N
Downward, 6.0 × 10⁵ N
Upward, 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ N

toLevel4.stem: A beam of protons curves upward in a magnetic field. If the beam were replaced with electrons at the same speed, in what direction would the electrons curve?
toLevel4.answer: Downward, because the negative charge reverses the force direction
distractors: Upward, because the force direction is the same for all charged particles
To the left, because electrons are deflected perpendicular to proton deflection
They would not curve because electrons are too light to be deflected by fields

toLevel4.stem: A positive charge moves to the right and a negative charge moves to the left, both through the same field directed into the page. Compare the force directions.
toLevel4.answer: Both experience forces in the same direction
distractors: They experience forces in opposite directions to each other
Only the positive charge experiences a magnetic force here
Only the negative charge experiences a magnetic force here

toLevel4.stem: An alpha particle (charge +2e) moves upward through a field directed to the right. A beta particle (charge −e) moves downward through the same field. Compare the force directions on each.
toLevel4.answer: Both particles experience forces in the same direction (out of the page)
distractors: The alpha particle is forced out of the page while the beta is forced into the page
The alpha particle is forced into the page while the beta is forced out of the page
Both particles experience forces in opposite directions (alpha left, beta right)

toLevel4.stem: In a cathode ray tube, electrons are deflected by a magnetic field. A student predicts the deflection direction but forgets to reverse for negative charge. What error does this introduce?
toLevel4.answer: The predicted deflection is in the opposite direction to the actual deflection
distractors: The predicted deflection magnitude is wrong but the direction is still correct
The prediction is correct because cathode ray tubes use conventional current rules
The prediction is correct because electrons follow the same rule as positive charges

toLevel4.stem: A negative ion with charge −2e moves into the page through a field directed to the left. What is the direction of the force?
distractors: Upward
To the right
Out of the page

toLevel4.stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field and curves to the left. If the field direction is reversed, what happens to the electron's path?
toLevel4.answer: The electron curves to the right instead
distractors: The electron continues to curve to the left
The electron travels in a straight line now
The electron spirals inward toward the centre

toLevel4.stem: A positive charge moving right through a field into the page is forced {{blank:1}}. An electron moving right through the same field is forced {{blank:2}}.
When a positive charge moves to the right and a negative charge moves to the {{blank:1}} through the same field, they both experience forces in the {{blank:2}} direction.
Reversing the magnetic field direction while keeping the charge's velocity the same will {{blank:1}} the direction of the force on {{blank:2}} charge type.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that instead of reversing the force for an electron, you can use a 'left-hand slap rule' directly. Evaluate whether this approach is valid.
toLevel5.answer: It is valid; a left-hand rule for electrons gives the same result as reversing the right-hand rule
distractors: It is invalid; only the right-hand rule can be used for any charged particle in physics
It is invalid; a left-hand rule would give a result perpendicular to the correct answer
It is valid; but only for electrons in uniform fields and not in non-uniform field shapes

toLevel5.stem: In a velocity selector, both positive and negative ions must travel the same straight path. Analyse why the magnetic force direction matters for this requirement.
toLevel5.answer: Positive and negative ions are deflected in opposite directions by the magnetic field, so only one sign of charge can be selected at a time
distractors: Both charge signs are deflected the same way so a velocity selector works for all ions equally
The magnetic force direction is irrelevant because only the electric field determines the path
Negative ions cannot enter a velocity selector because they are repelled by the entrance slit

toLevel5.stem: An electron and a positron (same mass, opposite charges) enter the same magnetic field at the same speed and angle. Compare their paths.
toLevel5.answer: They curve in opposite directions with identical radii, forming mirror-image circular paths
distractors: They follow the same path because they have the same mass and speed through the field
The electron curves tighter because negative charges interact more strongly with fields
The positron curves tighter because positive charges experience a stronger magnetic force

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why cosmic ray protons approaching Earth from the north are deflected eastward by Earth's magnetic field, while electrons from the same direction are deflected westward.
toLevel5.answer: The right-hand rule gives an eastward force on positive charges; the negative electron charge reverses this to westward
distractors: Protons are heavier than electrons so Earth's gravity deflects them in different directions
The magnetic field has different strengths on the east and west sides of the Earth's surface
Protons are attracted to the east magnetic pole while electrons are attracted to the west pole

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that the direction of force on a particle depends only on the charge sign, not on the velocity direction. Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect; the force direction depends on both the velocity direction and the sign of the charge
distractors: Correct; only the charge sign determines which way the particle is deflected by the field
Incorrect; the force direction depends only on velocity and is independent of the charge sign
Correct; the velocity only affects the magnitude of the force, not the direction of deflection

toLevel5.stem: In a mass spectrometer, ions of different masses but the same charge curve with different radii. If negative ions were used instead, how would the analysis change?
toLevel5.answer: The ions curve in the opposite direction but the radius relationship remains the same
distractors: Negative ions cannot be used in mass spectrometers because they are not deflected at all
The ions curve in the same direction because the detector accounts for the charge sign
Negative ions curve with larger radii because negative charges experience weaker forces

toLevel5.stem: Compare how you would determine the force direction on a doubly charged positive ion versus a singly charged negative ion moving through the same field.
toLevel5.answer: Apply the right-hand rule directly for the positive ion; reverse the result for the negative ion. Charge magnitude affects force size, not direction.
distractors: Apply the right-hand rule twice for the doubly charged ion and once reversed for the negative
Both ions experience forces in the same direction because the rule applies identically to all
The doubly charged ion follows the right-hand rule while the negative ion follows no rule

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate why it is a common exam error to forget to reverse the force direction for electrons, and suggest a reliable strategy to avoid this mistake.
toLevel5.answer: Students apply the rule for conventional current and stop; a reliable strategy is to always identify the charge sign before applying the rule
distractors: Students forget because the force is too small to observe, so they assume it does not matter
The error occurs because most textbooks do not mention the need to reverse for electrons
A reliable strategy is to ignore the charge sign and always use the left-hand rule instead

toLevel5.stem: An electron and a positron in the same field curve in {{blank:1}} directions, demonstrating that charge {{blank:2}} determines the force direction.
To avoid errors when applying the right-hand slap rule to negative charges, always {{blank:1}} the charge sign first, then {{blank:2}} the result if the charge is negative.
